claim: The $1,000 emergency withdrawal carries no 10% additional tax, so in the 12% bracket its cost is $120 of federal income tax (recoverable if the money is repaid to the plan within three years). Putting the bill on a card and paying it off in equal monthly payments, at the latest average rate on accounts charged interest (22.15% in 2026-05), costs $65.59 over 6 months and $124.0 over 12; the card interest passes the $120 tax only after 12 months. Across 127 quarterly rates since 1994-11, that crossover ranged from 11 months (at 23.37%, 2024-08) to 23 months (at 11.96%, 2003-02), median 18. For a 22% bracket worker the tax is $220 and the crossover is 22 months at today's rate (history: 21 to 41, median 33). Lost investment growth on the withdrawn money is not included. History, not a forecast.

assumptions: The worker's plan offers the emergency personal expense distribution and the worker qualifies (self-certified need, at least $2,000 vested so $1,000 is available, none taken in the last 3 years without repayment).

The whole $1,000 is taxed at the worker's federal marginal rate (12%, or 22% for comparison); no state income tax; the withdrawal is not repaid (if repaid within three years the tax can be recovered).
Card balance of exactly $1,000, no new charges, no fees, equal monthly payments; APR equal to the national average on accounts assessed interest at that observation, held fixed for the payoff period.
Lost investment growth on the $1,000 while out of the 401(k) is not counted; it would add to the withdrawal's cost.
Withholding at the time of withdrawal affects cash flow, not the final tax, and is ignored.
